text:
Predicates:
SpillsFoodOnClothing(x) ::: x spills a lot of food on their clothing.
NotablyTidy(x) ::: x is notably tidy.
ClumsyFoodie(x) ::: x is a clumsy foodie.
GoesOutFrequently(x) ::: x goes out frequently to find new food restaurants.
Cleanly(x) ::: x is cleanly.
ValuatesOrderAndSpotlessness(x) ::: x values order and spotlessness.
FamilyPrioritizesOrderAndSpotlessness(x) ::: x's family prioritizes order and spotlessness.
Peter(x) ::: x is Peter.

Premises:
∀x (SpillsFoodOnClothing(x) → ¬NotablyTidy(x)) ::: If people spill food on their clothing, then they are not notably tidy.
∀x (ClumsyFoodie(x) ∧ GoesOutFrequently(x) → SpillsFoodOnClothing(x)) ::: All clumsy foodies who go out frequently spill a lot of food on their clothing.
∀x (Cleanly(x) → NotablyTidy(x)) ::: If people are cleanly, then they are notably tidy.
∀x (ValuatesOrderAndSpotlessness(x) → Cleanly(x)) ::: If people value order and spotlessness, then they are cleanly.
∀x (FamilyPrioritizesOrderAndSpotlessness(x) → ValuatesOrderAndSpotlessness(x)) ::: All people whose families prioritize order and spotlessness themselves value order and spotlessness.
Peter(x) → ((SpillsFoodOnClothing(x) ∧ Cleanly(x)) ∨ (¬SpillsFoodOnClothing(x) ∧ ¬Cleanly(x))) ::: Peter is either a person who spills food and is cleanly, or does not spill food and is not cleanly.

Conclusion:
Peter(x) → ((ClumsyFoodie(x) ∧ GoesOutFrequently(x)) ∨ FamilyPrioritizesOrderAndSpotlessness(x)) ::: Peter is either a clumsy foodie who goes out frequently or someone whose family prioritizes order and spotlessness.
